extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political philosophy, civil liberty, and law
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply principles for when society or the State may legitimately interfere with individual conduct, distinguishing self-regarding acts from social acts and specifying permissible forms of prevention, regulation, and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of non-accountability for self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual is not accountable to society for his actions, in so far as these concern the interests of no person but himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society's proper responses to such conduct are limited to advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance; legal or social punishments are not justified when the action affects only the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of accountability for other-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: For such actions as are prejudicial to the interests of others, the individual is accountable and may be subjected either to social or to legal punishments, if society is of opinion that the one or the other is requisite for its protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference is legitimate when actions harm others; choice between social and legal sanctions depends on societal judgment and necessity for protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage/probability-of-damage is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage, or probability of damage, to the interests of others can alone justify interference, but it does not always justify such interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some harms arising from legitimate pursuit of ends (e.g., winning a contest) are accepted by society; interference is reserved for means contrary to general interest (fraud, treachery, force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means vs ends: interference justified when means are wrongful
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositions of interest do not justify interference unless means of success involve fraud, treachery, or force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society tolerates competitive losses unless procured by unjust means; regulation should target wrongful methods rather than outcomes alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade as a social act and limits of market regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade is a social act; sellers affect others and therefore fall within society's jurisdiction, but cheapness and quality are best ensured by leaving producers free under buyers' equal freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some regulation (fraud prevention, sanitary measures, worker protections) is legitimate, broad controls (price-fixing, making commodities hard to obtain) can unjustifiably infringe liberty—especially the buyer's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegitimacy of making commodities difficult to obtain
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences intended to make it impossible or difficult to obtain a particular commodity (e.g., Maine Law, prohibition of importation) are objectionable because they infringe the buyer's liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations that effectively prevent access to goods infringe individual liberty even if aimed at producers or sellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police preventive function vs risk of abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Government has an undisputed preventive function to take precautions against crime before it has been committed, but this function is more liable to be abused than its punitory function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervention is warranted when someone is evidently preparing to commit a crime; mere possibility of delinquency is insufficient because almost any freedom could be framed as facilitating crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible preventive measures should minimize liberty infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Precautions that prevent crime without substantial infringement on legitimate uses are preferable (e.g., labelling dangerous drugs) while measures that make legitimate use impossible (e.g., universal medical certificates) are excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'preappointed evidence' (formalities/records) to deter misuse—registries, recorded buyer purpose, third-party presence—since these raise obstacles to criminal misuse without barring legitimate access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing certainty from mere danger in paternalistic interference
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is certainty that an action will cause harm (e.g., person attempting to cross an unsafe bridge with no time to warn), others may forcibly prevent it; but when only danger exists, the person should ordinarily be warned, not coerced, unless incapable (child/delirious/etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paternalistic coercion is justified only in cases of clear incapacity to judge or imminent, certain harm; otherwise respect individual judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted legal restrictions for repeat harmful behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that is self-regarding (e.g., drunkenness) is generally not fit for legislative interference, but a person who has once committed violence while intoxicated may lawfully be placed under special personal legal restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor restrictions to individuals with proven propensity to harm others (e.g., increased penalties or restrictions tied to prior convictions) rather than blanket bans on private conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on punishing mere idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Idleness is not a proper subject of legal punishment except in persons receiving public support or when idleness constitutes a breach of contract or legal duty (e.g., failure to support children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where legal obligations to others are not met, compulsion (e.g., compulsory labour) is not tyrannical if no other means achieve fulfilment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of public indecency while tolerating private conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts directly injurious only to agents may be legally prohibited when done publicly, as publicity converts them into offences against others (offences against decency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between private liberties and offenses arising from public exhibition; law may rightly address the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to advise and instigate where conduct is permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever it is permitted to do, it must be permitted to advise to do; exchange of opinions and suggestions about self-regarding matters should be free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle is complicated when the instigator derives personal benefit (professionally promoting harmful conduct); then regulation may be justified to exclude interested solicitations that subvert impartial choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating profit-driven instigation and public facilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: While acts like fornication and gambling must be tolerated, professions or establishments that promote them for gain (pimping, public gambling-houses) sit on the boundary and may be regulated or prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are arguments on both sides; restrictions aim to prevent organized or profit-incentivized promotion while leaving private conduct free, but enforcement can be imperfect and may drive activities underground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting commodities for taxation on welfare grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation of stimulants or other consumables may be justified insofar as the State must levy indirect taxation and should select commodities consumers can best spare; selection a fortiori should prefer commodities whose excessive use is injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxation up to the point producing maximum revenue (given fiscal needs) is admissible and can be approved as consistent with public policy rather than mere prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of places of public resort and licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Places of public resort require police restraint; sale of potentially harmful commodities for on-site consumption may be confined to persons of known respectability, subject to opening-hour regulations and licence withdrawal if breaches of peace occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation aimed at public surveillance and preventing locations from becoming centres for crime is legitimate; however, limiting numbers of outlets primarily to reduce access is not, unless aimed at effective supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on restrictions intended to infantilize labouring classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting access to commodities (e.g., beer-houses) to treat labouring classes as children and fit them for freedom is unjustifiable; such measures reflect a paternalistic, despotic approach incompatible with free institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts should be exhausted to educate people for freedom rather than to govern them by restraint; only after such efforts and demonstrable incapacity might stricter measures be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of voluntary regulation among consenting individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty implies a corresponding liberty for any number of individuals to regulate by mutual agreement matters that concern only them, so long as the will of all implicated persons remains unaltered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual agreements should generally be kept, but exceptions exist where engagements violate third-party rights or are injurious to the parties themselves; the law often refuses to enforce contracts that amount to sale of oneself (slavery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on alienation of one's freedom (contracts abhorrent to liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: An engagement by which a person should sell himself as a slave is null and void; the principle of freedom cannot require that he be free not to be free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts that permanently alienate basic liberties are unenforceable because the very justification for freedom (future choice) would be defeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and legal considerations where contracts affect third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person's promise has encouraged reliance by another, or has led to consequences affecting third parties (e.g., marriage producing children), obligations to those third parties arise and must weigh on decisions to release from engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if legal freedom to retract exists, moral obligations toward affected third parties are significant and must be considered; law may treat monetary contracts differently from personal-service or relational contracts.
